t: How To Handle Parents Who Want To Talk And Talk https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2020/03/21/how-to-handle-parents-who-want-to-talk-and-talk/
q: When a parent approaches to talk, always say kindly, “How can I help you?” This causes them to get right to the point and lets them know that you remain in teacher mode even outside the presence of students.
Being available to parents anytime they wish opens the door to being taken advantage of. While some will be respectful of your time, others will exploit it for all its worth.
Closing it is a form of saying no, which is a key to being a happy and effective teacher. It allows you to focus efficiently on your work, so you can head home to recharge.
Gossiping with parents will always come back to bite you. Because, if they’re gossiping with you, they’re also gossiping with others—revealing your juicy news and scuttlebutt.

Being friends with parents, at least as long as their child is in your class, will cause you to be less than impartial. Even if you fight against this tendency, it will affect your assessment of their child.
Maintaining a professional stature does take some discipline, but it makes your teaching life so much easier. It frees up your time. It eliminates drama and stress.
x: Recommends opening any parent conversation with 'How can I help you?' to keep interactions focused and signal professional mode.

Suggests closing the classroom door at day's end as a subtle, effective signal that you are unavailable.

t: How To Get Your Students To Feel Remorse For Misbehavior
q: There must be no doubt among your students what does and doesn’t constitute breaking each rule. Thus, you must define your boundaries precisely.
Your job isn’t to accept shoddy performance, do their work for them, or let them off the hook. It isn’t to threaten, beg, or implore them to behave or give effort.
If you aren’t consistent, then you’re communicating to your students that none of the above is true. You’re telling them very clearly that your rules don’t even matter enough for you to follow them.
Shifting responsibility for listening, learning, and behaving over to your students reframes misbehavior entirely. It makes it seem immature, absurd, even embarrassing.
It isn’t thrust upon them as a guilt trip, which then is summarily rejected. It isn’t an outside force they can ignore, deny, or refuse to acknowledge.
No, it comes from inside the student. Where real change happens.
x: Recommends defining classroom rules with total precision so that breaking them is unmistakably a student's own choice.
Insists teachers should model that their job is to deliver world-class lessons, not to beg, threaten, or manage misbehavior.
Frames consistent follow-through as essential; inconsistency signals to students that the rules don't actually matter.
Argues that authentic student remorse requires shifting responsibility for behavior onto students rather than lecturing or guilting them.
Linsin argues that genuine student remorse comes not from teacher lectures or guilt trips but from shifting responsibility for behavior squarely onto students themselves.

t: A Quick Way To Calm Your Class, Build Rapport, And End Bullying
q: If you’re ever bullied, bothered, or made fun of, or feel uncomfortable in this classroom in any way, I promise to fix it. You can send me an email, slip me a note, or ask to speak with me privately.
Rest assured, I’ll move mountains to take care of the problem so you can feel safe to learn and enjoy being in this class.
When you extend kindness to your students, and boldly promise their protection from the scourge of bullying, or any other impediment to learning, they’ll want to pay you back in spades.
The statement, you see, puts you on notice. It exerts a soft pressure to fulfill your promises. Thus, you must follow through.
The statement also puts bullies on notice that if they do engage in hurtful behavior, there will be heck to pay.
That they can count on you to be a leader they can trust. Maybe the only one they’ve ever known.
x: Notes the statement also puts potential bullies on notice that they can no longer act without consequence in the shadows.
